description: We care about Artemis Lunar Landing Sites
summary: The project is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. Choosing a site means balancing sunlight for power against Earth visibility for communication, and specialist tools make quick comparisons hard. My app pulls Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons for each site and shows them side by side: sunlit and Earth-visible time, longest dark period, longest Earth outage, and the share of arrival times that allow an unbroken six-day surface stay. A sky view with a time slider and sunset and Earthset countdowns shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon. A GNSS layer adds a question most tools skip: when could Earth’s GPS and Galileo signals reach the site? That question matters for future lunar navigation, following NASA’s LuGRE experiment. The tool is open, reproducible and clear about its limits.
details:
What it does. The app lets planners, students and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates. For each site it shows how much of the time the Sun and Earth are above the horizon, the longest dark period and Earth outage, and the share of possible arrival times that allow an unbroken multi-day stay with both available. A sky-view dial with a time slider shows the Sun and Earth relative to the horizon, with countdowns to sunset and Earthset. A GNSS layer shades the periods when Earth is up and at least one GPS or Galileo satellite is geometrically placed to send a signal toward the Moon.

How it works. Python scripts pull hourly Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation from JPL Horizons for each surface point and cache them. A metrics module computes the comparison numbers. The GNSS layer propagates current GPS and Galileo orbits with skyfield, takes the Moon’s position from the DE421 ephemeris, and counts satellites inside an assumed main-lobe cone that aren’t blocked by Earth. A Streamlit app presents everything.

Benefits and impact. It speeds up early screening of sites and dates, including when a schedule slips, and gives students a clear view of why the Moon’s south pole is hard. It also frames GNSS availability as a landing-site factor.

Tools. Python, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, skyfield, requests, Streamlit.

Creativity and care. The GNSS layer is the new element. Sites come from published studies with citations, and I screen them against thresholds those studies use. I tested the GNSS result at three cone angles (20°, 23.5°, 26°) to show how sensitive it is. Limits are stated plainly: the horizon is a smooth sphere without terrain, GNSS is geometry only, and orbit elements limit the window to about a month.
